title: Closed-profile validation of a pasted entviz SVG does not bind declared cell data to what the SVG actually paints, so a crafted reference reaches an affirmative `identical` verdict while displaying a different value
impact: The primary asset of the whole component — the machine `identical` verdict (comparison-design.md §3, §6.2 adjudication S3: "an SVG whose <text> says X while its ink shows Y could otherwise reach IDENTICAL with no preimage") — is forgeable with no hash work. A victim who recognizes the picture (the entviz premise) AND gets a green `= Identical` chip is holding a value that is not the one the artifact depicts, which is exactly the substitution the tool exists to prevent.
description: `validateClosedProfile` blesses attacker-authored SVG markup (arriving from paste / drop / file-pick / URL-fetch via EntvizCompare.classifyResult → compareSvg) using only a tag whitelist plus `on*=`/`style=`/`@font-face`/external-`href`/external-`url()` checks; it never constrains paint order, `<defs>`, `opacity`/`display`/`visibility`/`fill`, `transform`, or duplicate per-cell content, so the `data-*`/`<text>` channels that compare.ts then trusts need not be the channels a viewer renders — and compareSvg turns that trust into `{ state: "identical" }` at line 274.
exploit_scenario: 1. Attacker generates `A = render(V_victim)` with the public library and `B = render(V_attacker)` at the same size/shape. 2. In `B`, the attacker renames the non-rendering annotation attributes (`data-channel="cell"` → `data-x="cell"`, `data-color-bar-band` → `data-x-band`, drops `data-truncated`); this changes no pixels. 3. The attacker appends B's inner content (an opaque `<rect>` cover plus B's `<g>/<rect>/<path>/<text>` groups — every tag is in CLOSED_PROFILE_TAGS) just before `</svg>` of `A`. 4. `validateClosedProfile` returns true (no comments, no forbidden tag, no `on*`/`style`/`href`/non-`#` `url()`), `parseEntvizSvg` sees only A's genuine, fully self-consistent cell groups, so refText, surroundBits and colorBarLetters all match and compareSvg returns `{ state: "identical" }`. 5. Every viewer paints B over A, so the human sees entviz(V_attacker) while the tool certifies it as equal to V_victim. Variants that need even less editing: put A's cell groups inside the whitelisted `<defs>` (never painted), or give A's `<text>` `opacity="0"`/`display="none"`/`transform="translate(-9999,0)"` — none of which are rejected, although §6.2 item 1 explicitly requires rejecting `transform` on text and extra per-cell instances.
preconditions: The attacker can supply the reference SVG the victim compares against (paste, drop, file, or a URL the victim fetches) — the documented threat assumption at compare.ts:125-127
The attacker knows the value the victim has entered (typically because the attacker supplied it, or it is public)
The victim's trust in the artifact comes from seeing it rendered (any SVG viewer/browser), which is the artifact's purpose
recommendation: Do not treat a declared channel as trustworthy unless it is provably the one painted. Concretely: (a) reject any element outside the exact structural shape of a conformant entviz rather than a flat tag whitelist — no content after/over the grid, no `<defs>` content other than the clipPath the renderer itself emits, no second `<g data-channel="cell">` for an index already seen, and no more than one `dominant-baseline="central"` `<text>` per cell group (compare.ts:179-186 currently takes the first and ignores the rest); (b) reject presentation attributes that can hide or displace painted content (`opacity`, `fill-opacity`, `display`, `visibility`, `transform`, `clip-path`) anywhere in the document, and reject `<!DOCTYPE`/internal entity subsets; (c) scope the `data-color-bar-band` scan (compare.ts:214) to the color-bar group instead of the whole string; and (d) if declared-vs-painted cannot be enforced by parsing alone, downgrade the SVG engine's ceiling from `identical` to `unknown·similar` and route to the human walk.

title: compareSvg blesses an attacker-authored SVG as `identical` — the closed-profile gate never binds declared cell text to the ink that renders
impact: The tool's single security-bearing output — the user's belief that a reference artifact equals their value — can be forged. A reference SVG whose visible glyphs render value Y while its declared cells declare value X yields a green "= Identical" chip (or, for >512-bit inputs, the green "≈" `unknownSvgSimilar` chip via chipFor, EntvizCompare.ts:217-222) against X. Because EntvizCompare deliberately never embeds the pasted markup ("The reference is ALWAYS re-rendered through our own <Entviz>", EntvizCompare.ts:495-498), the victim never sees the discrepancy inside the tool: they saw the attacker's picture elsewhere (mail, web page, PDF) and the tool certifies it as their value.
description: The untrusted source is the reference SVG the user acquires from an attacker (paste / file-drop / URL-fetch, EntvizCompare.ts:106-127 → compareSvg); the sink is the `identical` verdict at compare.ts:274, which is derived exclusively from the SVG's *declared* `<text dominant-baseline="central">` and `data-surround-bits` / `data-color-bar-band` attributes (parseEntvizSvg, compare.ts:192-218). Nothing ties those declarations to what the document actually paints, and `validateClosedProfile` (compare.ts:151-168) whitelists `rect`/`path`/`text`/`tspan`/`polygon`/`g` with arbitrary geometry, `fill`, `opacity`, `display` and `transform` attributes, so extra ink and hidden declarations both pass.
exploit_scenario: Mallory takes the genuine `render(X)` output for the well-known value X, appends an opaque `<rect fill="#ffffff" .../>` over the grid plus fresh `<text>` elements drawing the tokens of her own value Y (or simply marks the honest cell groups `display="none"`). Every element and attribute used is inside the closed-profile whitelist, so validateClosedProfile returns true; parseEntvizSvg extracts the untouched declared cells for X; refText === myText and the recomputed surround bits / colour-bar letters agree, so compare.ts:274 returns `{state:"identical"}`. Alice, who saw the artifact rendering Y on Mallory's page, drops the file into the comparator, is told it is identical to X, and accepts Y.
preconditions: Victim uses the SVG reference path (paste / drop / file-pick / URL-fetch) — the default, intended acquisition flow
Attacker knows the value the victim will compare against (e.g. a published key or address), which is the §2.4 attacker-chosen-reference threat the design already assumes
Value classifies as <=512 bits for a flat `identical`; larger values still reach the green `≈` similar chip
recommendation: Do not treat a validated closed-profile SVG's declarations as trustworthy without binding them to the ink. Implement the design's own §6.2 requirements: reject `transform` (and `display`/`visibility`/`opacity`) on cell text, reject any drawing element that is not part of the recognized cell/colour-bar structure ("extra per-cell instances"), and re-render the recovered value through the tool's own renderer, comparing the produced markup (or its raster) against the reference before any `identical`/`similar` verdict.

title: Unbounded quadratic BigInt decode in characterize() — the 64 KiB anti-DoS cap is never applied on this path
impact: CPU exhaustion / hang. A ~10 MB value pins one core for minutes-to-hours; in the browser it freezes the tab that was asked to display the attacker's identifier, in Node (a server rendering entvizes, or the conformance CLI) it stalls the process. Even at the render()-capped 65536 chars the loop is ~2e8 limb operations, a >1000x amplification over the input size.
description: `characterize(entropy)` (characterize.ts:553) takes a fully attacker-controlled identifier string and applies NO length cap of its own, then feeds the whole `parsed.core` into this accumulator loop; BigInt multiply-by-small is O(limbs), so the loop is O(N^2) in the input length.
exploit_scenario: An attacker supplies an "identifier" of ~10 MB consisting of `z1` repeated. Every specific parser in PARSE_FUNCS declines it (all are anchored and length-bounded or prefix-bound), so `parse()` falls through to `detectAlphabetByDisproof`, which returns BASE58 ('z' rules out hex, '1' rules out base32 and bech32). `characterize()` then calls `sizeBitsFor` -> `decodedBytesInteger`, which builds a ~59-million-bit BigInt one digit at a time. Because `<EntvizPill>` calls `characterize(value.trim())` at EntvizPill.ts:307 before it calls `render(value, opts)`, render()'s MAX_INPUT_CHARS guard (entviz.ts:1854) never gets a chance to reject the input — the tab hangs first.
preconditions: The host passes an untrusted value to `characterize()` or to `<EntvizPill value=...>` — precisely entviz's documented 'wild / adversarial' use case (trust.ts:1-23)

The value is composed only of base58 characters that are not all-hex, all-base32 and not all-bech32 (e.g. the two-character repetition `z1` repeated), so `detectAlphabetByDisproof` (entviz.ts:1327) labels it `base58`, which is in `INTEGER_DECODE_ALPHABETS`
recommendation: Enforce `MAX_INPUT_CHARS` at the top of `characterize()` (and of every public entry point) before `parse()` runs, and replace the digit-at-a-time BigInt accumulation with a size estimate: for base58/base36/decimal, `ceil(core.length * log2(base) / 8)` gives the same byte count without materializing the integer, or chunk the accumulation. Do not rely on `render()`'s cap to protect siblings that are called first.

title: Generic bech32 parser drops the HRP from the identity-bearing core, so two different bech32 identifiers (e.g. nostr `nsec1…` and `npub1…`) render the same entviz and machine-compare as `identical`
impact: The entviz for `npub1<52 data chars><cksum>` and for the corresponding `nsec1<same 52 data chars><cksum'>` is identical in every fingerprint-driven channel (cells, nucleus colors, surround bits, ellipse, color bar, blank map); `comparisonText()`/`describeChannels()` are byte-identical, and `compareValues`, `compareComparisonText` and `compareSvg` all return the affirmative verdict `{state:"identical"}`. Only the small gray top-label prefix slot ("npub1" vs "nsec1") differs. A user who relies on the glyph or on the tool's "identical" verdict to confirm "this is my public key, safe to publish" can be led to publish the secret key. The same collision covers cross-chain / role variants of one cosmos-style payload (`cosmos1…` vs `cosmosvaloper1…` vs any other HRP), because the HRP is the only free variable and the 6-char checksum is trivially recomputable for any HRP the attacker picks.
description: Untrusted identifier text reaches `parseBech32`, which puts only `data.slice(0,-6)` in `core` and marks the human-readable part a presentation prefix (`prefixSemantic` omitted ⇒ false). Everything the verification surface is built from — `computeFingerprint(fingerprintCore(core, prefix, prefixSemantic))` at entviz.ts:1861, the cell text, and `identityKey` in compare.ts:46 — therefore ignores the HRP, so two distinct bech32 strings that share a payload verify as the same value.
exploit_scenario: An attacker (or an honest mistake amplified by the tool) presents a bech32 string whose HRP differs from the expected one but whose data payload is identical — e.g. the victim's own `nsec1…` where an `npub1…` is expected, or `otherchain1<payload>` where `cosmos1<payload>` is expected. Constructing it requires no brute force: strip the last 6 chars, substitute the desired HRP, recompute the bech32 polymod (the same `bech32ChecksumConst` this file implements). The victim compares the two values with `<EntvizCompare>`/`compareValues` or by glancing at the two pills; the grids, colors, surround patterns and read-aloud comparison text match exactly and the engine reports `identical`, so the substituted identifier is accepted.
preconditions: The value is a generic bech32 string not claimed by an earlier parser (i.e. not bc1/tb1/ltc1/addr1/stake1 — those keep the checksum inside the core and are unaffected)
The two colliding values share the same data payload, which is the normal case for nostr npub/nsec/note and for one key expressed under different cosmos-SDK HRPs
The human or host relies on the glyph / comparisonText / compareValues verdict rather than on a byte comparison of the raw strings
recommendation: Make the HRP identity-bearing for bech32: either return `prefixSemantic: true` so `fingerprintCore` folds `"<hrp>1" ‖ core` into the primary fingerprint (the treatment already given to did/urn/gitoid/swhid), or keep the full `data` (checksum included) in `core` as `parseBitcoin`'s SegWit branch already does — the checksum binds the HRP. Either fix propagates automatically to the cells, the fingerprint, `comparisonText`, and `identityKey`.
snippet: return { type: "bech32", core: data.slice(0, -6), alphabet: BECH32, prefix: `${hrp}1`, suffix: data.slice(-6) };

title: `identityKey` discards every non-semantic prefix, so `compareValues` returns the affirmative `identical` verdict for demonstrably different identifier strings
impact: `compareValues("nsec1<payload><ck>", "npub1<payload><ck'>")` → `{state:"identical"}`; `compareValues("1220<digest>", "1b20<digest>")` (sha2-256 vs keccak-256 multihash of the same bytes) → `identical`; an SSH ed25519 body relabelled with the RSA structural header → `identical`. The comparison engine is the component the UI turns into a green affirmative verdict, so a wrong `identical` here is the failure mode the whole product exists to prevent. This finding is bounded by the fact that the attacker cannot substitute arbitrary key material — the colliding pair always shares the victim's payload — so the achievable confusions are key-role (secret vs public), chain, and hash-algorithm.
description: Both compared strings are fully attacker-supplied and flow into `classifyInput`; `identityKey` then deliberately drops the presentation prefix (bech32 HRP, multihash hash-function header, SSH algorithm header, base58 version char), so the equality test at compare.ts:73 emits `{state:"identical"}` — the tool's strongest affirmative claim — for two different values. Reported here as well as at the parser because this line is independently fixable (it could include `c.prefix` even while the render keeps its current keying).
exploit_scenario: A host embeds `<EntvizCompare>`/`compareValues` to let a user confirm a pasted value against a reference. The user pastes their nostr `nsec1…` where the reference is the matching `npub1…` (a well-known nostr footgun, and one an attacker can deliberately induce with "paste the key that matches this picture"). The engine reports `identical` with no caveat, and the user proceeds to share the secret key.
preconditions: Caller uses the exported `compareValues` / `compareComparisonText` / `compareSvg` API (re-exported from @entviz/core via `export * from "./compare.ts"`)
The two values differ only in a prefix the parser classifies as presentation (bech32 HRP, multihash header, SSH algorithm header)
recommendation: Include the literal presentation prefix in the identity key (`JSON.stringify([c.core, c.alphabet.name, c.prefix, c.prefixSemantic])`), or — preferably — fix the parsers so those prefixes are bound into the fingerprint, which keeps the invariant the comment relies on ("two inputs that render the same entviz compare identical") true in the safe direction rather than the unsafe one.

title: compareComparisonText affirms `identical` from the cell-text channel alone, which omits the identity-bearing prefix — two different values verdict as a match
impact: A machine-certified affirmative equality verdict — the product's primary security assertion — between two values the same module classifies as different. The victim accepts a substituted identifier.
description: The untrusted source is the pasted reference comparison-text (`referenceText`, arriving via EntvizCompare.classifyResult:117 from paste/drop/file/fetch); the sink is the affirmative `{state:"identical"}` security verdict at compare.ts:97, which is reached on a cell-text match only. Cell text is derived solely from `core` + `alphabet` (tokenizeEntropy), while the engine's own identity definition (`identityKey`, compare.ts:37-47) also includes the semantic prefix — so a DID-method / URN-NID substitution produces the same comparison text and a false affirmative.
exploit_scenario: A vendor publishes the entviz "comparison text" for `did:good:AbCdEfGhIjKlMnOpQrStUvWx`. An attacker gets the victim to hold `did:evil:AbCdEfGhIjKlMnOpQrStUvWx` — same method-specific id, an attacker-controlled method that resolves to an attacker-controlled document. The victim pastes the published comparison text into <EntvizCompare>. `compareValues` correctly returns `different` (the semantic prefix differs), but `classifyResult` then falls through to `compareComparisonText`, whose cell readout is byte-identical for both values (tokens come only from the core, and with an exactly-full grid there is no fingerprint permutation or blank pattern to disagree). The engine returns `identical`; the UI shows the green `=` verdict and, because `refValue: value`, re-renders the reference figure from the victim's OWN value, erasing the visual difference (background colour, colour bar, ellipse, surround bits all actually differ).
preconditions: The reference is acquired as text that is not itself a parseable value (so `compareValues` fails first and control falls through to the comparison-text branch at EntvizCompare.ts:117)
The user's value and the attacker's value share the same normalized `core` + alphabet and differ only in an identity-bearing prefix (DID method, URN NID)

The token count exactly fills the chosen grid (e.g. 4 or 6 tokens — the common 128-bit / UUID / 24-char-msid case), so `assignCellIndices` returns the identity map and no fingerprint-driven blank shifts appear in the readout
recommendation: The comparison text is not an identity proof because it carries neither the prefix nor the alphabet. Either (a) return `unknown` (route to the human walk) whenever `classifyInput(value).prefixSemantic` is true, or (b) make the canonical comparison text carry the rendered label/prefix and require it to match, or (c) require a digest-derived channel (colour-bar letters / surround bits) to agree before affirming.

title: "Complete" walk plan drops every gestalt check for <=512-bit values, so a prefix-only difference reaches the "no difference found" affirmative
impact: A human-verification affirmative ("you read every cell, a full visual check") for two demonstrably different values, presented as a stronger check than the machine verdict it contradicts.
description: `includeGestalt = d.truncated` means a Complete walk over a non-truncated value contains only text steps; the affirmative sink `liveVerdict` (compare-walk.ts:347) then reaches `no-difference` from cell-text agreement alone. Cell text is prefix-independent (tokenizeEntropy uses only `core`+`alphabet`), while every channel that binds the identity-bearing prefix (background, colour bar, ellipse, quartiles, blank map — all SHA-512-digest driven) is exactly what was removed.
exploit_scenario: The victim pastes `did:evil:AbCdEfGhIjKlMnOpQrStUvWx` as the reference against their own `did:good:AbCdEfGhIjKlMnOpQrStUvWx`. The machine chip correctly reads "≠ Different", so the victim launches the offered guided walk to double-check. With 6 filled cells the value is `small`, so only "Complete" is offered; its plan contains six text steps and nothing else. Each step spotlights one cell with a 50%-opacity scrim over everything outside the focus ring, and asks only "Do the highlighted characters match?" — every cell does match. After the third answer `liveVerdict` flips to `no-difference`, and the walk ends with "No difference found — you read every cell, a full visual check.", directly contradicting the correct machine verdict and hiding the genuinely different background/colour-bar/ellipse channels behind the scrim.
preconditions: Reference and value share a core+alphabet and differ only in the identity-bearing prefix (DID method / URN NID)
The value is <=512 bits (`d.truncated === false`)
The user runs the "Complete" walk — which is the ONLY mode offered for a small value (EntvizCompare.ts:729-731 and EntvizWalk.ts:325 both suppress spot-check when filled cells <= 6)
recommendation: Do not treat the text channel as identity-complete: include the gestalt dimensions in a Complete plan whenever the value carries an identity-bearing prefix (`classifyInput(value).prefixSemantic`), or unconditionally, since gestalt is the only channel that binds prefix||core.

title: Attacker-supplied "comparison text" reference yields a false `identical` verdict for two different identifiers (identity-bearing prefix/alphabet are not in the compared channel)
impact: Defeats the component's primary asset — the user's belief that two values are equal. The UI shows the green `=` "Identical — the same value" chip (chipFor, EntvizCompare.ts:207) for two genuinely different identifiers, and because `refValue: value` is returned the tool re-renders OUR OWN figure as the reference (EntvizCompare.ts:498, 798), so the human side-by-side cross-check and any subsequent guided walk compare value-against-itself and cannot catch the difference.
description: The untrusted reference string (pasted/dropped/fetched) is routed to `compareComparisonText`, which compares only the grid cell TEXT (`packages/core/src/compare.ts:93`) and returns `{state:"identical"}` for a non-truncated match; that channel omits the semantic prefix and the alphabet name that the module's own `identityKey` (`compare.ts:46`) treats as identity, so two values the engine itself calls `different` can produce byte-identical comparison text and be reported as the strongest affirmative verdict.
exploit_scenario: Alice holds `did:key:z6Mkha…` (48-char msid → 12 tokens → full 3x4 grid, no blanks). Mallory mints `did:mallory:z6Mkha…` with the identical method-specific id and sends Alice the comparison text of his DID (the readout the tool itself promotes for out-of-band checking). Alice pastes it into <EntvizCompare>. `compareValues` correctly reports `different` (the semantic prefix is part of `identityKey`), but `compareComparisonText` compares only the 12 cell tokens — which are derived from the shared core and are identical — and returns `identical`. Alice sees the green `=` "Identical — the same value" banner plus two identical figures, and accepts Mallory's DID, which resolves to key material Mallory controls.
preconditions: The attacker supplies the reference as comparison text (an officially supported reference format — 'Copy comparison text', pastePrompt, and the read-aloud ceremony)

The victim's value and the attacker's value share the same normalized core and tokenize identically (e.g. `did:key:<msid>` vs `did:<attacker-method>:<same msid>`, or `urn:a:X` vs `urn:b:X`, or a bare base58 key vs `did:key:<same chars>`)
The value's token count exactly fills the chosen grid so there are no fingerprint-placed blank cells (e.g. 12 tokens = a 45-48 char base64url msid → 3x4 grid; also 4, 6, 9, 16 tokens)
The value is <=512 bits (a truncated input returns `unknown` instead)
recommendation: Do not let a comparison-text match alone reach `identical`. Either (a) include the identity-bearing fields in the compared channel (bind the readout to `identityKey`'s tuple — normalized core + alphabet name + semantic prefix — e.g. by prefixing the canonical readout with the rendered label/prefix and comparing that), or (b) demote a comparison-text match to `{state:"unknown", similar:true}` (walk-to-confirm) whenever `classifyInput(value).prefixSemantic` is true or the reference cannot be reconstructed into a value whose `identityKey` matches. Add a regression test for `did:a:X` vs `did:b:X` and for a bare core vs `did:key:<core>`.
snippet: if (asCmp.state !== "different") return { kind: "verdict", verdict: asCmp, refValue: value };

title: EntvizPill calls characterize() on the raw value before render()'s MAX_INPUT_CHARS cap, exposing an O(n^2) BigInt decode to an unbounded attacker-controlled string
impact: Availability. A single pill rendering an attacker-chosen value freezes the browser's main thread (React renders this memo synchronously), making the host page unresponsive; under SSR the same call blocks the rendering worker. The guard that was supposed to bound this (`MAX_INPUT_CHARS`, explicitly commented as an "Anti-DoS cap") never runs because `characterize` is invoked before `render`.
description: The untrusted `value` prop (documented as content the host did not author) is handed to `characterize()` first, and `characterize` has no length guard; core's anti-DoS cap (`MAX_INPUT_CHARS`, entviz.ts:1854) only fires later inside `render()`, so the quadratic BigInt accumulator in `decodedBytesInteger` (characterize.ts:97-110) runs on strings the cap was written to reject.
exploit_scenario: An attacker publishes a credential/document whose identifier field is a ~1 MB run of base58-only characters that is not valid hex/base32/bech32 (e.g. repeated "9i"). A viewer's app renders it in an <EntvizPill>. `characterize(value.trim())` classifies it as base58 (entviz.ts:1327-1336) and `sizeBitsFor` routes to `decodedBytesInteger`, which performs one BigInt multiply-add per character against an accumulator that grows to ~6 million bits — roughly n^2/2 limb operations. The tab hangs before `render()` ever reaches the 65536-character rejection at entviz.ts:1854. I did not execute this code, so the wall-clock cost is reasoned from the algorithm, not measured.
preconditions: Host renders <EntvizPill value={...}> with a value it does not control (the documented use case: identifiers pulled out of credentials/documents)

The value is classified into a non-power-of-2 alphabet (base58 is reachable through the disproof detector, e.g. a long run of characters containing both '9' and 'i', which disproves hex, base32 and bech32)
No length pre-check by the host before passing the value
recommendation: Apply the same `MAX_INPUT_CHARS` guard at the top of `characterize()` (and in `classifyInput`'s parsed branch, which today caps only the UTF-8 fallback path), or have EntvizPill reject/short-circuit over-long `value` before the memo runs. Alternatively bound `decodedBytesInteger` (it only needs a byte length, which can be computed as ceil(len*log2(base)/8) for oversized inputs).

title: URL fetch follows redirects while the shown/recorded provenance origin is the pre-redirect origin
impact: The provenance string — which the component deliberately locks as non-overridable judgment-bearing copy (VERDICT_LOCKED_KEYS, lines 262-266) — and the `fetch.success` event both misreport where the reference bytes came from, so a user (or a host logging the firehose) attributes attacker-controlled reference content to a trusted origin. The verdict engines are unaffected; the damage is limited to provenance/consent integrity.
description: `refOrigin` is parsed from the user-pasted URL and shown as the pre-fetch consent hint (line 676) and later as the locked provenance label, but `fetch()` uses the default `redirect: "follow"` and nothing re-derives the origin from `res.url`, so bytes returned from an arbitrary redirect target are attributed to the origin the user approved.
exploit_scenario: A victim is told to fetch a reference entviz from `https://trusted.example/r?u=…`, an open redirect. The pre-fetch hint and the post-fetch label both read "From trusted.example", while the SVG/value actually served came from the attacker's host via the 302. The user believes a trusted party vouched for the reference they just compared against.
preconditions: `allow.url` enabled (default) and the user pastes a URL and clicks Fetch
The pasted URL's origin hosts a redirect the attacker controls (open redirect, or an attacker-chosen URL the victim was talked into pasting)
No host `fetchReference` is injected (the built-in fetch path)
recommendation: Re-derive the origin from the response (`new URL(res.url).origin`) and use that for `setRef({origin})` and the `fetch.success` event; or pass `redirect: "error"`/`"manual"` and require a fresh user confirmation showing the new origin before following a cross-origin redirect.
